title: Review: Protein structure and function; Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CE02b#t4 term and clue written for the game; CE02a#t3 term and clue written for the game; CE02a#t2 term and clue written for the game; CE02a#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM08a#N.10b, CE02a#N.11b, CE02b#N.7c, BM08a#N.13, CE02a#N.12, CE02b#N.3, BM08a#N.12b, CE02a#N.8b, BM08a#N.4b. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Turgid
items.clue: Firm, because water has entered the vacuole and its contents press on the wall

items.label: Lysosome
items.clue: Single-membrane vesicle full of hydrolytic enzymes; digests worn-out organelles

items.label: Golgi apparatus
items.clue: Stack of curved, flattened membrane sacs that modifies proteins and packages them

items.label: Cristae
items.clue: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, giving a large surface area for making ATP

questions.stem: A strong acid is added to a solution of an enzyme that normally works at about pH 7, lowering the pH to 1. The enzyme loses all of its activity. Which statement best describes what has happened to the enzyme?

options.text: Its peptide bonds are broken, so it has been split up into its separate amino acids.
It has been killed by the acid, in the same way that a strong acid kills living cells.
It is inhibited but not denatured, as only high temperature can denature enzymes.
Its folded shape is disrupted, although its amino acids are still joined in sequence.
They are membrane-bound organelles, so they are found only in eukaryotic cells.
They copy the DNA of genes into mRNA, which then carries the copy to the cytoplasm.
They build the cell's proteins inside the nucleus, close to the genes that code for them.
They are made of rRNA and protein and are found in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

questions.explanation: Ribosomes are non-membrane structures made of ribosomal RNA and protein, found in the cells of all forms of life, where they synthesize proteins according to mRNA sequences.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes vacuoles in animal cells?

options.text: Animal cells have no vacuoles, as vacuoles are found only in the cells of plants.
Animal cells have many vacuoles, smaller than in plant cells, that store materials.
Animal cells have one large central vacuole that keeps them firm by turgor pressure.
Animal cells have many small vacuoles, which are sacs that hold water and nothing else.

questions.explanation: In animal cells, vacuoles are smaller and more plentiful than in plant cells, and they store cellular materials.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids
The changed amino acid supplies less energy to the reaction, so the substrate cannot react

questions.stem: An electron micrograph of a cell shows a large amount of rough ER, a large Golgi and many small vesicles close to the cell surface. What does this cell most likely do?

options.text: It makes large amounts of lipid, using the ribosomes on its ER.
It digests engulfed bacteria, using the enzymes in its many vesicles.
It makes proteins, such as enzymes, and releases them from the cell.
It makes proteins in the Golgi, which the ER then packs into vesicles.

questions.explanation: RER makes proteins; the Golgi modifies and packages them; vesicles carry them to the surface for release.

questions.stem: Which statement about cell walls is correct?

options.text: In bacteria, fungi and plants, the cell wall gives a structural boundary and blocks some substances.
In plants, the cell wall rather than the plasma membrane controls which solutes enter the cell.
In plants, the cell wall stops water from entering, so plant cells do not swell in pure water.
Cell walls are found around plant cells but usually not around those of fungi or bacteria.

questions.explanation: Cell walls of Bacteria, Archaea, Fungi and plants provide a structural boundary and a permeability barrier for some substances; water and many small solutes still pass through.

questions.stem: A hypothetical enzyme has its highest rate of reaction at 40 °C. At 45 °C, its rate is lower. Which statement best explains the lower rate at 45 °C?

options.text: Enzyme and substrate molecules move so fast that they pass each other before they are able to bind.
Some hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape are disrupted, so the active site fits less well.
Some peptide bonds between the enzyme's amino acids break, splitting its chain into pieces.
Some of the enzyme molecules have been killed by the heat, so fewer are left alive to react.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how the structure of a mitochondrion's inner membrane allows ATP to be synthesized efficiently?

options.text: Its many folds form pockets that store ATP until the rest of the cell needs it.
Its folds give a large surface area for membrane-bound steps that make ATP.
It is smooth, so ATP can pass quickly out through the folded outer membrane.
Its many folds give room to create the energy that is then stored in ATP.

questions.explanation: The inner membrane is highly convoluted. Its folds increase its surface area, so more of the membrane-bound steps of ATP synthesis can take place at once.

questions.stem: Alpha-helices are found in many proteins whose amino acid sequences are very different from one another. Which statement best explains why alpha-helices can form in polypeptides with such different sequences?

options.text: A helix is held by bonds between R groups, and every kind of R group can form those bonds equally well.
A helix forms wherever the folding chain happens to coil at random, whatever the sequence.
A helix is formed by the peptide bonds, which join neighboring amino acids together in every chain.
A helix is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms, which are present whatever the R groups are.
